title: Saykally v. Commissioner
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit
subject: Section 174 Deductions: Self-Funded Research Licensed to the Owner's Corporation
summary: Saykally v. Commissioner, 247 Fed. Appx. 914 (9th Cir. 2007), affirming T.C. Memo. 2003-152, holds that an individual software developer who personally funds research to license the resulting technology to his wholly owned corporation acts as a passive investor, not in connection with his own trade or business, so his IRC Section 174 R&D deductions are disallowed.
metaDescription: Saykally v. Commissioner (9th Cir. 2007): a developer funding research for his own corporation is a passive investor, so IRC § 174 deductions fail.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background

The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit's decision in Saykally v. Commissioner, 247 Fed. Appx. 914 (9th Cir. 2007), affirming the United States Tax Court's memorandum opinion in David M. and Teri L. Saykally v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2003-152, 85 T.C.M. (CCH) 1401 (2003), stands as a critical cautionary precedent in federal research and development (R&D) tax jurisprudence. The ruling delineates the strict statutory boundaries governing when an individual software developer, founder, or intellectual property holder may claim research and experimental (R&E) deductions under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 174—and, by statutory extension, the R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41. At its core, Saykally establishes that an individual taxpayer who funds software development in their personal capacity with the intent to license the resulting technology to a separate corporation for marketing and distribution—even when that corporation is wholly owned by the taxpayer—is acting as a passive investor rather than operating "in connection with a trade or business".
Factual Narrative and Taxpayer's Claim

The dispute originated from the commercial activities of David M. Saykally, an executive and technologist with extensive experience and technical familiarity in the computer software industry. In 1991, Computer Power Group Limited (CPG), a large Australian professional services company that provided computer programmers to create business software and was also involved in the worldwide marketing of several lines of business software applications, retained Saykally on a short-term contract basis as a consultant to identify why CPG was losing money on the marketing of its software applications and how to stop such losses. Following Saykally's consulting assessment, CPG attempted to hire him to implement his recommendations; instead, the parties agreed to move the marketing of CPG's software out from under CPG, and Saykally organized his own corporation, Computer Power Software Group, Inc. (CPSG), in November 1992, of which he owned all outstanding shares and served as president, chief operating officer, and sole director. On August 10, 1993, Saykally, CPSG, and CPG entered into a Software Marketing and Management Agreement (with a retroactive effective date of September 30, 1992) under which CPSG licensed certain rights to market CPG's existing software products (InTEXT, Today, and Operating Control Systems) through three CPSG subsidiaries. In exchange for the software marketing rights, CPSG agreed to pay ongoing royalties to CPG.

Under the initial business model, ongoing software research and development necessary to sustain the product line was to be financed by three Australian R&D syndicates that had historically funded CPG's software development. However, in or about May 1995, CPG informed CPSG that the syndicates' development funding would terminate in July 1995, and on July 7, 1995, the syndicates notified CPSG to cease and desist marketing CPG's software technology, taking the position that CPSG had no rights to the technology they had funded because they had not approved the management agreement. The syndicates' development funding terminated in or about July 1995, leaving the planned software development unfinished and without any new marketable products, so that without additional funding CPSG and its subsidiaries would lose their existing customers.

Faced with the reality that CPSG would collapse without continuous software development, Saykally elected to assume sole personal responsibility for funding and directing the R&E in his individual name. Saykally's decision to conduct the development in his own name rather than in the name of his wholly owned corporation was driven primarily by negotiating considerations—he believed that personal ownership of the developed technology would give him more negotiating leverage over CPG and the syndicates (CPG could cancel the submarketer agreement, and the syndicates claimed they could modify or terminate CPSG's rights)—as well as by the facts that CPSG, as a marketing entity, had neither development capability nor the financial resources to fund the development. To formalize this arrangement, Saykally executed a written contract with CPSG dated October 1, 1995, under which he covenanted to provide software research and development in his reasonable discretion and at his sole expense, while retaining all rights, title, and interest in the resulting "developed technology". Simultaneously within the same contractual framework, Saykally granted CPSG the right to market and license the developed technology to end-users in exchange for royalty payments.

Although Saykally structured the R&E as an individual undertaking on paper, the underlying financial mechanics relied heavily on corporate conduits. Saykally intended to finance the individual R&E expenditures by borrowing funds directly from CPSG. Because CPSG did not have sufficient cash to advance all the development costs, Saykally arranged for CPSG to borrow funds from Uniplex Software, Inc.—a related entity 50.1 percent owned by CPSG Ventures, a general partnership in which Saykally held a 70 percent interest—which advanced a total of $1.15 million to CPSG in 1996 ($750,000 on February 5 and $400,000 on July 11). During taxable years 1995 and 1996, CPSG, by and through its wholly owned subsidiaries, directly paid $67,543 and $1,361,006, respectively, in research and development expenses on Saykally's behalf. On their joint federal individual income tax returns (Form 1040, Schedules C, Profit or Loss From Business), David and Teri Saykally claimed IRC Section 174 R&D deductions of $67,534 for taxable year 1995 and $1,421,645 for taxable year 1996, alongside various other Schedule C business expense deductions across taxable years 1994, 1995, and 1996.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

Upon examination, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue disallowed the entirety of the claimed Section 174 R&D deductions ($67,534 for 1995 and $1,421,645 for 1996), asserting that Saykally did not pay or incur the expenditures "in connection with his trade or business". The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) did not dispute that the expenses were research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense or that the amounts were reasonable; its position was that Saykally did not pay or incur the expenses in connection with his own trade or business and lacked the objective intent to prospectively enter into his own trade or business with the developed technology, which he intended to license to CPSG for use in CPSG's existing business.

Additionally, the Commissioner disallowed a portion of the general business expenses claimed on the taxpayers' Schedules C (for a consulting business named "CPSG Ventures") for taxable years 1994 and 1996—adjustments of $18,241 and $25,731, respectively—on the ground that the taxpayers had not established a business purpose for the expenses, while allowing deductions to the extent the expenses were reimbursed by CPSG (no Schedule C expense disallowance was at issue for 1995, for which the Commissioner allowed $22,275 more than claimed). Finally, the Commissioner determined accuracy-related penalties pursuant to IRC Section 6662 for all three audit years (1994, 1995, and 1996), citing negligence, disregard of rules or regulations, and substantial understatement of income tax, including a penalty specifically targeting an erroneously claimed double deduction.
Governing Statutory and Judicial Framework

In the United States federal tax system, the deductibility and creditability of research expenditures are governed by the interlocking provisions of IRC Sections 174, 41, and 162, alongside the penalty regime of Section 6662. During the tax years at issue, Section 174(a)(1) permitted a taxpayer to elect to treat R&E expenditures paid or incurred during the taxable year "in connection with his trade or business" as current deductions rather than capitalizing them to a capital account. Under administrative guidance such as Rev. Proc. 2000-50, the IRS recognized that the process of computer software development closely parallels research and experimentation, allowing software development costs to be treated symmetrically with Section 174 expenses, provided the foundational statutory trade or business requirements are satisfied.

While IRC Section 162(a) requires a taxpayer to be actively "carrying on" an existing trade or business to deduct ordinary and necessary business expenses, the U.S. Supreme Court held in Snow v. Commissioner, 416 U.S. 500 (1974), that the phrase "in connection with" under Section 174 is more permissive, allowing startup enterprises to deduct R&E costs prior to commencing active operations or generating revenue. However, in Green v. Commissioner, 83 T.C. 667 (1984), the Tax Court curtailed abusive reliance on Snow, holding that a taxpayer who intends solely to license resulting inventions in exchange for royalties is merely a passive investor and never enters a trade or business. Building upon Snow, the courts—including the Tax Court in Diamond v. Commissioner, 92 T.C. 423 (1989), affd. 930 F.2d 372 (4th Cir. 1991)—have tempered its expansive reading by requiring that a taxpayer not currently engaged in a trade or business demonstrate a "realistic prospect" of subsequently entering into its own trade or business utilizing the technology developed, a standard the Ninth Circuit (to which Saykally was appealable) applied in Kantor v. Commissioner, 998 F.2d 1514 (9th Cir. 1993), and Scoggins v. Commissioner, 46 F.3d 950 (9th Cir. 1995). Satisfying the "realistic prospect" standard requires proof of both an objective intent to enter into the business at the time the expenses are incurred and the operational capability of doing so.

This trade or business analysis is reinforced by the distinction drawn in tax law between engaging in one's own business and investing in the business of another, recognized in Whipple v. Commissioner, 373 U.S. 193 (1963), and Higgins v. Commissioner, 312 U.S. 212 (1941), and applied in Kantor, under which a taxpayer's existing or prospective business must be its own and not that of another entity (while Commissioner v. Groetzinger, 480 U.S. 23 (1987), cited by the court, requires that a trade or business be pursued with continuity and regularity and primarily for income or profit). An individual shareholder who incurs expenses to protect or enhance the value of their wholly owned corporation acts in the capacity of an investor and cannot attribute the corporation's trade or business to themselves to claim individual deductions.

Furthermore, Section 174 eligibility serves as the statutory gateway to the federal R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41. To qualify for the credit under Section 41, a taxpayer's activities must satisfy the Four-Part Test under Section 41(d)(1), where the very first prong—the "Section 174 Test" under Section 41(d)(1)(A)—mandates that the expenditures must be eligible to be treated as expenses under Section 174. Moreover, Section 41(b)(1) imposes an even stricter threshold than Section 174, requiring that qualified research expenses (QREs) be paid or incurred in "carrying on" any trade or business of the taxpayer, which excludes mere passive licensing or investment. Consequently, a taxpayer in Saykally's position, who fails the "in connection with a trade or business" standard under Section 174, would necessarily be barred from claiming the Section 41 R&D tax credit, although the Saykally opinion itself does not address Section 41.
The Court's Final Holding

In an opinion authored by Judge Ruwe and subsequently affirmed by the Ninth Circuit, the court ruled predominantly in favor of the Commissioner. Both the Tax Court and the Ninth Circuit held that Saykally was not entitled to deduct the $67,534 (1995) and $1,421,645 (1996) R&D expenditures because the evidentiary record demonstrated that, at the time the expenses were incurred, he lacked an objective intent and a realistic prospect of entering into a future trade or business of his own involving the developed software. Because his purpose was to create developed technology that he would license to CPSG for use in CPSG's existing business—he intended that the developed technology would be marketed through CPSG—his activities amounted to nothing more than those of a prudent investor rather than a trade or business operator. Although CPSG alleged in its petition that it would be entitled to the R&D deductions if the Saykallys were not, CPSG abandoned that argument (and the parties conceded that there was no deficiency or overpayment for CPSG), so the court expressed no opinion on CPSG's potential entitlement.

With respect to the non-R&D deductions, the court sustained the IRS's disallowance of the Schedule C business expenses at issue for 1994 and 1996 (amounts claimed in excess of the expenses reimbursed by CPSG). The court rejected Saykally's procedural argument that the Commissioner failed to adequately specify which deductions were denied, reaffirming that the burden of proof rests squarely on the taxpayer to substantiate all claimed deductions with credible documentary evidence. Finally, the court issued a split ruling on the Section 6662 accuracy-related penalties. The court held that the Saykallys were not liable for the Section 6662 penalties attributable to the disallowed Section 174 R&D deductions, finding that it could not conclude that they acted unreasonably in claiming those deductions because the facts of the case were unique and Saykally testified that he relied upon the advice of a tax professional. Conversely, the court upheld the Section 6662 penalties attributable to the unsubstantiated Schedule C deductions for 1994 and 1996, finding that the taxpayers failed to show they were not negligent, as well as the penalty relating to the erroneously claimed double deduction of a $60,000 charitable contribution to the Granite Bay Montessori School on the 1996 return (claimed as $120,000), holding that the Commissioner's imposition of that penalty was substantially justified.
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

A rigorous forensic deconstruction of Saykally v. Commissioner reveals five interconnected legal, contractual, and evidentiary failures that destroyed the taxpayer's position. These deficiencies highlight the exact structural and documentation traps that snare closely held technology companies, software founders, and R&D ventures during IRS examinations and federal appellate litigation.
Failure to Prove Objective Intent and Realistic Prospect of an Independent Trade or Business

The primary legal failure in Saykally was the taxpayer's inability to satisfy the two-pronged "realistic prospect" test established by the Ninth Circuit in Kantor and Scoggins. While Saykally possessed unquestionable personal technical competence in the software industry—having previously consulted for CPG and, during the development, monitored the Australian development team, helped solve technical programming problems, prioritized programmers' tasks, and participated in beta testing—personal technical expertise alone does not convert an individual into an active trade or business.

Under Scoggins, a pre-operational taxpayer claiming Section 174 deductions must establish both an objective intent to use the research results in their own future trade or business and the operational capability to do so. As the Ninth Circuit emphasized in Kantor, while the probability of a taxpayer going into its own business satisfies Section 174, the mere possibility of doing so does not. In Saykally, the evidentiary record was devoid of any objective proof—such as an independent business plan, direct customer acquisition infrastructure, a dedicated sales force, distribution channels, or manufacturing and hosting capabilities held in Saykally's individual name—indicating that Saykally intended to personally commercialize and market the software. Instead, the court found that Saykally's purpose was to create developed technology that could be licensed to CPSG, Inc. for use in its existing business; all publications and marketing materials relating to the developed technology were created on behalf of CPSG, and the taxpayers themselves argued on brief that CPSG was in the best position to market the new products. As the Tax Court held (and the Ninth Circuit affirmed), where the record shows that a developer's R&D activities amounted to no more than the development of property rights intended to be licensed to another entity—here, his wholly owned corporation—for use in that entity's business, the developer acts as an investor and is not entitled to a current Section 174 deduction.
Contractual Licensing Traps and Pre-Operational Disposition of Commercial Rights

Saykally's legal position was fatally compromised by the terms of the written R&D and licensing contract he executed with CPSG. Under that agreement, while Saykally retained nominal legal title to the developed software technology in exchange for funding the R&E at his discretion, he simultaneously granted CPSG the right to license and market the technology in exchange for royalty payments.

In federal R&D tax law, courts examine all contracts and agreements in the record to determine whether the researcher reasonably anticipated availing itself of the rights it possessed on paper, and agreements that effectively relinquish commercialization of the research results to another entity at the outset can defeat a realistic prospect of entering one's own business (as in Kantor), although such a grant is not automatically fatal (as in Scoggins). In Saykally, the development agreement granted CPSG only a nonexclusive license, and the court did not decide whether the contractual arrangements deprived Saykally of the capability to use the fruits of the research (noting only that his right to use the developed technology was questionable); instead, it relied on the agreements, a CPSG board resolution authorizing him to undertake research on CPSG's behalf, and his own testimony to find that he lacked the objective intent to use the developed technology in a business of his own. The Tax Court relied on Green v. Commissioner and Spellman v. Commissioner—cases involving passive research partnerships that funded R&E for exploitation by others—for the principles that a deduction is never appropriate where the taxpayer acts solely in an investor capacity and that the management of investments is not a trade or business for purposes of Section 174. Although exploitation of inventions through royalties or patent sales can theoretically constitute a trade or business if conducted with substantiality, continuity, and regularity across multiple independent sources (as noted by the IRS Office of Chief Counsel in Legal Advice Issued by Field Attorneys, LAFA 20055203F), in Saykally the taxpayers did not allege, and the court could not find, that Saykally's own activities during the period the R&D expenditures were made were sufficient to constitute a trade or business, and there was no evidence that he marketed the developed technology himself.
Entity Attribution Fallacy and Strategic Abandonment by the Corporate Conduit

A critical conceptual error committed by Saykally was conflating his personal legal identity with that of his wholly owned corporation, CPSG. When the Australian syndicates' development funding terminated and the syndicates challenged CPSG's marketing rights, Saykally conducted the R&E in his individual name to create intellectual property ownership outside of CPSG and thereby gain negotiating leverage over CPG and the syndicates, while still intending for CPSG to survive and market the product.

However, under federal tax law, a taxpayer who chooses the advantages of the corporate form—or who deliberately separates assets from a corporation for litigation protection—must accept the tax consequences of that structural separation. Because CPSG was a separate corporation filing its own federal income tax return, CPSG's active software marketing trade or business could not be attributed to Saykally individually. When Saykally funded research to keep CPSG from going out of business, he incurred those expenses in his capacity as a shareholder and investor protecting his capital investment in CPSG, not in connection with an individual sole proprietorship.

Compounding this structural flaw was a major litigation and procedural failure. CPSG itself was a petitioner in the consolidated Tax Court proceedings; it had initially deducted the R&D costs on its federal income tax return for the year ended September 30, 1996, then amended that return to eliminate the deduction (which the Saykallys then claimed individually), and in its petition it alleged that if the Saykallys were not entitled to the R&D deductions, CPSG was. However, CPSG abandoned this alternative argument, and the parties conceded that there would be no deficiency or overpayment for CPSG, so Judge Ruwe expressed no opinion on CPSG's entitlement, and the approximately $1.49 million claimed was not allowed as a current deduction to either the individual or the corporation in these proceedings (under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-1, R&D expenditures not deductible under Section 174(a) must be charged to capital account).
Circular Intercompany Financing and Tax-Avoidance Shifting

Although the Tax Court did not rest its holding on the financing arrangements, the record shows that the R&D expenses were paid through related-party financing mechanics. Rather than expending personal capital from an independent sole proprietorship bank account, Saykally relied on CPSG and its wholly owned subsidiaries to actually disburse $67,543 in 1995 and $1,361,006 in 1996 on his behalf. Moreover, because CPSG lacked the cash reserves to fund these disbursements, Saykally arranged for CPSG to borrow $1.15 million in 1996 from Uniplex Software (an entity 50.1 percent owned by CPSG Ventures, in which Saykally held a 70 percent interest), while Saykally memorialized his own indebtedness to CPSG with an unsecured, interest-bearing promissory note of up to $1.4 million dated October 1, 1995, under which he was personally liable for the amounts CPSG expended.

In subsequent administrative analysis (specifically IRS LAFA 20055203F), the IRS Office of Chief Counsel highlighted Saykally as a textbook example of an improper attempt to avoid taxes by shifting R&E expenditures among related parties to an individual taxpayer who could immediately utilize the tax deductions on a personal return, even though the individual had no intention of using the R&E results in an individual business. Furthermore, the discrepancy between the amounts paid by CPSG on Saykally's behalf ($67,543 in 1995 and $1,361,006 in 1996) and the amounts claimed by Saykally on Schedule C ($67,534 in 1995 and $1,421,645 in 1996) is explained by the record rather than by any finding of the court: for 1995 the parties stipulated a deduction of $67,543 while the return and notice of deficiency state $67,534, and the 1996 Schedule C amount included $60,967 of interest expense (of which the parties agreed $30,020 was not deductible on Schedule C but was deductible as investment interest); the court did not rely on these differences or make any finding about accounting segregation, noting instead that CPSG used its accounting system to track the costs.
Documentary Substantiation Failures, Procedural Missteps, and Penalty Bifurcation

Beyond the Section 174 issue, Saykally committed severe evidentiary errors regarding the general Schedule C business deductions at issue for 1994 and 1996. Under IRC Section 6001 and Tax Court Rule 142(a), deductions are a matter of legislative grace, and the taxpayer bears the affirmative burden of proving entitlement to every claimed deduction through contemporaneous books, records, invoices, and receipts. Instead of introducing granular accounting ledgers and source documents to substantiate the Schedule C expenses, Saykally relied on incomplete copies of credit card statements and his own vague testimony that all the expenses were for business purposes, and also argued that the Commissioner's notice of deficiency and court papers failed to give notice of which specific deductions were denied. The Tax Court rejected this argument (and the Ninth Circuit affirmed), reasoning that the Commissioner had allowed the expenses to the extent CPSG reimbursed them, that the taxpayers were in the unique position to know which expenses had been reimbursed—so the disallowed amounts were simply the difference—and that the taxpayers failed to detail the expenses denied, their amounts, and their business purpose, including items such as computer equipment and cellular telephones that, as listed property, require strict substantiation under Section 274(d).

The ruling also illustrates the nuanced operation of IRC Section 6662 accuracy-related penalties and the IRC Section 6664(c) reasonable cause exception. With respect to the approximately $1.49 million in disallowed Section 174 R&D deductions, Saykally avoided the 20% accuracy-related penalty because the court could not find that the taxpayers acted unreasonably in claiming the deductions, given that the facts of the case were unique and Saykally testified that he relied upon the advice of a tax professional. Conversely, the court sustained the Section 6662 penalties on the unsubstantiated Schedule C deductions for 1994 and 1996 and on the erroneously claimed double charitable contribution deduction for 1996. Good-faith reliance on tax counsel protects complex legal interpretations regarding the contours of Section 174 trade or business nexus, but it does not excuse basic recordkeeping negligence or claiming the same $60,000 charitable contribution twice (a $120,000 deduction), an error the court found a prudent taxpayer would have been warned of, and for which the adequate-disclosure rules of Rev. Proc. 96-58 provided no protection against the negligence component of the penalty.
Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and judicial requirement examined in Saykally v. Commissioner (and its direct interplay with IRC Section 41) against the taxpayer's specific factual and evidentiary failures and the governing judicial standard of proof established by the Tax Court and the Ninth Circuit.

headers: Court's Standard of Proof & Evidentiary Mandate

cells: Trade or Business Nexus for R&E Expenditures
IRC § 174(a)(1); Snow v. Commissioner, 416 U.S. 500 (1974)
Claimed $67,534 (1995) and $1,421,645 (1996) on individual Schedule C while intending that his wholly owned corporation (CPSG) market the developed technology in its existing business.

Taxpayer must prove via objective facts that R&E expenses were paid or incurred "in connection with" the taxpayer's own existing or future trade or business, not merely as a passive investor or licensor.
"Realistic Prospect" of Entering a Future Business
Kantor v. Commissioner, 998 F.2d 1514 (9th Cir. 1993); Scoggins v. Commissioner, 46 F.3d 950 (9th Cir. 1995)

Relied on personal software industry expertise, but the record contained no evidence—not even his own testimony—that he intended to engage in a business of his own with the developed technology, no specific plans or forecasts, and no evidence that he marketed it himself; the court decided the case on the intent prong and did not reach capability.

Pre-operational taxpayers must prove both (1) an objective intent to enter their own business using the research results, and (2) the operational capability to do so; mere possibility is insufficient—probability is required.
Active Commercialization vs. Passive Licensing
Green v. Commissioner, 83 T.C. 667 (1984); Spellman v. Commissioner, 845 F.2d 148 (7th Cir. 1988)
Executed an upfront contract with CPSG exchanging R&E funding for title while simultaneously granting CPSG marketing and licensing rights for royalties.

Contracts and agreements are examined as evidence of the parties' expectations; where, at the time of the research, the taxpayer's activities were unlikely to amount to more than those of an investor (e.g., developing property rights to license to another entity for use in its business), the deduction is denied; whether activities are sufficiently substantial and regular to constitute a trade or business is a factual determination.
Corporate Entity Separateness & Non-Attribution
Higgins v. Commissioner, 312 U.S. 212 (1941); Whipple v. Commissioner, 373 U.S. 193 (1963); Kantor v. Commissioner, 998 F.2d 1514, 1519 (9th Cir. 1993)

Assumed R&E individually to gain negotiating leverage in the dispute with CPG and the Australian syndicates and prevent wholly owned CPSG from failing, then claimed deductions personally while CPSG abandoned its claim.

A corporation's trade or business cannot be attributed to its sole shareholder; a shareholder who develops property rights to license to his wholly owned corporation for use in its business acts as an investor, and R&D expenditures not deductible under § 174(a) must be charged to capital account (Treas. Reg. § 1.174-1).
Economic Substance & Intercompany Payment Tracing
IRC § 174(a); Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2; IRS LAFA 20055203F

CPSG and its subsidiaries directly paid $67,543 (1995) and $1,361,006 (1996) funded in part by $1.15 million that the related Uniplex Software advanced to CPSG in 1996; after CPSG amended its return to eliminate its own deduction, Saykally claimed the deductions on his personal return, where the 1996 deduction substantially eliminated an approximately $1.4 million capital gain from the sale of Unify Corp. stock.

The court did not decide the case on payment-tracing or economic-substance grounds: Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(8) permits deduction of research carried on in the taxpayer's behalf by another, and Saykally was personally liable on an interest-bearing note; the IRS (in non-precedential LAFA 20055203F) later cited Saykally as an instance of shifting R&E expenditures among related parties to a person who could use the deduction but did not intend to use the results in its own business.
Cascading Eligibility for the R&D Tax Credit
IRC § 41(a), § 41(b)(1), § 41(d)(1)(A); Rev. Proc. 2000-50

By failing the threshold "in connection with a trade or business" test under § 174(a) for lack of objective intent, the activities would necessarily also fail the § 174 test of § 41(d)(1)(A) and the stricter "carrying on" requirement of § 41(b)(1), although the court's opinion does not address § 41.

To claim QREs under IRC § 41, expenditures must first qualify under IRC § 174 (§ 41(d)(1)(A)), be incurred in actively carrying on a trade or business (§ 41(b)(1)), satisfy the Four-Part Test, and not constitute funded research (§ 41(d)(4)(H)).
Substantiation of General Business Deductions
IRC § 162(a); IRC § 6001; Tax Court Rule 142(a)

Failed to adequately substantiate the disallowed Schedule C expenses for 1994 and 1996 (offering only incomplete credit card statements and self-serving testimony); argued that the IRS failed to identify which specific deductions were disallowed and that the expenses were sufficiently substantiated.

The Commissioner's deficiency determination is presumed correct; the taxpayer bears the affirmative burden of producing contemporaneous source documents (invoices, ledgers, canceled checks) tying each expense to a business purpose.
Accuracy-Related Penalties & Reasonable Cause

Claimed invalid § 174 deductions based on professional advice (penalty abated), but failed to substantiate other Schedule C deductions for 1994 and 1996 and claimed a $60,000 charitable contribution twice ($120,000) on the 1996 return (penalties sustained).

Under § 6664(c), reasonable cause and good faith are determined case by case on all facts and circumstances (Treas. Reg. § 1.6664-4(b)(1)); the court found the taxpayers did not act unreasonably on the unique § 174 issue given testimony of reliance on a tax professional, but negligence includes failure to keep adequate records or substantiate items (Treas. Reg. § 1.6662-3(b)(1)), and a prudent taxpayer would have been warned by an extra $60,000 deduction; Rev. Proc. 96-58 adequate disclosure does not apply to the negligence penalty.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial holdings of Saykally v. Commissioner into actionable legal and technical tax strategy, the following two applied industry case studies examine realistic commercial scenarios that mirror the exact pitfalls encountered in the ruling. Each case study provides a comprehensive, step-by-step remedial blueprint covering project governance, contract restructuring, technical documentation, and experimentation tracking to ensure full compliance with IRC Sections 174 and 41.
Case Study 1: Enterprise Cloud Database Spin-Off Facing Founder-Level IP Isolation and Related-Party Licensing Pitfalls
Baseline Scenario and Legal Vulnerability

Dr. Marcus Vance, a prominent distributed-systems architect, is the sole shareholder of Vance Data Systems, Inc. (VDS), a C corporation that markets legacy enterprise relational database software. VDS becomes embroiled in a contentious intellectual property and royalty lawsuit with a European venture syndicate that previously co-funded VDS's legacy codebase. To prevent VDS from losing market share while shielding next-generation intellectual property from the European syndicate's legal claims, Dr. Vance forms an individual sole proprietorship (reported on Schedule C via a disregarded single-member LLC, Vance Labs LLC) to develop "Project Hyperion"—a novel, autonomous cloud-native graph database engine.

Mirroring the exact defective structure in Saykally, Dr. Vance executes a short agreement between Vance Labs LLC (himself individually) and VDS, whereby Dr. Vance retains legal title to Project Hyperion's source code but grants VDS an immediate right to market, distribute, and license Project Hyperion to enterprise clients in exchange for a 15% gross revenue royalty. Vance Labs LLC has no sales personnel, no marketing budget, no independent customer support infrastructure, and no cloud hosting contracts in its own name. Because Dr. Vance lacks personal liquidity to pay the $1.8 million annual engineering payroll and cloud compute costs for Project Hyperion, VDS borrows $1.8 million from an institutional lender (Apex Capital) and pays the software engineers and cloud vendors directly on Dr. Vance's behalf, recording the disbursements as an informal shareholder loan. On his personal Form 1040 (Schedule C), Dr. Vance claims $1.8 million in Section 174 R&E deductions and calculates an IRC Section 41 R&D tax credit, while also deducting unitemized travel and consulting expenses across both VDS and Schedule C.

Under Saykally, Kantor, and Green, an IRS examination will result in the complete disallowance of Dr. Vance's individual Section 174 and Section 41 claims. Because VDS holds the commercialization and marketing rights from inception, Dr. Vance has no "realistic prospect" or objective intent of entering an independent trade or business involving Project Hyperion. Furthermore, VDS's direct payment of expenses using borrowed third-party funds invites the IRS to characterize the arrangement as a shifting of deductions among related parties to an individual investor, as the IRS Office of Chief Counsel later described Saykally in LAFA 20055203F.
Step 1: Project Governance and Entity Restructuring

Rather than isolating the intellectual property in a passive individual Schedule C proprietorship, Dr. Vance must align the entity incurring the R&E expenditures with an active trade or business—or a pre-operational entity with an ironclad, independent "realistic prospect" of commercialization—prior to incurring research costs. First, if Dr. Vance seeks pass-through tax treatment, he should establish Vance Labs LLC as an operating partnership (under Subchapter K) or an S corporation that is structurally equipped to operate its own commercial software-as-a-service (SaaS) trade or business. To satisfy the dual Scoggins and Kantor requirements, Vance Labs must adopt a formal Corporate Charter and a Board-Approved Three-Year Commercialization Business Plan demonstrating both the objective intent and operational capability to market Project Hyperion directly to enterprise customers via cloud marketplaces. Vance Labs must hire or contract its own fractional Chief Revenue Officer, maintain its own commercial website, and register its own merchant billing accounts so that its commercial capability is probable rather than merely possible. Alternatively, if VDS must remain the sole marketing and distribution entity, VDS—not Dr. Vance individually—must be the taxpayer claiming the Section 174 deductions and Section 41 credits. To achieve litigation ring-fencing without losing tax benefits, VDS can form a wholly owned special-purpose subsidiary or enter into a qualified contract research agreement under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(10) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e) where VDS incurs the expenditures in connection with its existing active software marketing business, thereby avoiding CPSG's fatal procedural error in Saykally of abandoning the corporate-level claim.
Step 2: Contractual Terms and Economic Substance Remediation

Assuming Vance Labs operates as an independent R&D and commercialization entity, all related-party agreements with VDS must be purged of pre-operational exclusive marketing grants. Dr. Vance must immediately rescind the simultaneous licensing agreement with VDS because, as Saykally and Kantor illustrate, courts examine such agreements as evidence of the developer's expectations, and an arrangement under which an existing corporation is expected to market the technology (in Kantor, an option to acquire exclusive marketing rights for a nominal sum) undermines the developer's "realistic prospect" of independent business entry. If VDS is later utilized as one of several distribution channels, any non-exclusive reseller or distribution agreement must be negotiated at arm's length under IRC Section 482 only after Vance Labs has established its own direct-to-market SaaS licensing capability and multiple independent revenue streams, aligning with the taxpayer-favorable facts in IRS LAFA 20055203F. Simultaneously, the parties must eradicate the circular intercompany payment conduits. VDS must cease paying engineers or vendors on Vance Labs' behalf. If third-party financing from Apex Capital is required, Vance Labs must borrow directly from Apex Capital, or Dr. Vance must execute a documented, interest-bearing promissory note with bona fide repayment schedules, deposit the capital directly into Vance Labs' dedicated operating bank account, and disburse all W-2 wages, contractor fees, and cloud computing invoices directly from Vance Labs' accounts.
Step 3: Technical Documentation and Process of Experimentation Tracking

To secure both Section 174 eligibility and the Section 41 R&D tax credit, Vance Labs must contemporaneously document that Project Hyperion satisfies the statutory Four-Part Test under IRC Section 41(d)(1). First, to satisfy the Permitted Purpose and Technological in Nature prongs under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and (C), the engineering leadership must document in a formal Software System Architecture Specification that Project Hyperion seeks to improve the functionality, query performance, and fault-tolerance reliability of distributed graph databases, relying strictly on principles of computer science, distributed consensus algorithms, and non-volatile memory management. Second, to prove the Elimination of Technical Uncertainty under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a), project charters must record the exact capability and methodological uncertainties existing at the project's outset—specifically, that conventional database architectures cannot achieve sub-10-millisecond ACID-compliant transaction commits across multi-region cloud nodes without severe lock-contention bottlenecks. Third, to substantiate a structured Process of Experimentation under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5), the engineering team's Agile/Jira and Git repositories must be configured to systematically log algorithmic hypotheses (such as evaluating a novel lock-free optimistic concurrency control protocol against a modified Raft consensus algorithm), automated load-testing simulations, and benchmark telemetry demonstrating why initial memory-indexing prototypes failed under 100,000 concurrent write operations per second and required iterative architectural redesigns.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Financial Substantiation and Penalty Insulation

To prevent the Schedule C substantiation failure and double-deduction penalties sustained in Saykally, Vance Labs must implement an enterprise resource planning (ERP) general ledger with discrete cost centers separating qualified Section 174 and Section 41 R&D wages, supplies, and cloud hosting expenses (under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2) from ordinary Section 162 business expenses and VDS's corporate expenses. Every non-R&D business expenditure must be backed by digitized vendor invoices, receipts, and documented business purpose logs pursuant to IRC Section 6001. Finally, prior to filing, an independent CPA firm must perform an intercompany reconciliation audit across Dr. Vance's personal return, Vance Labs' return, and VDS's corporate return to verify that zero duplicate deductions exist across entities or schedules, accompanied by a formal written tax opinion from a specialized R&D tax attorney satisfying the reasonable cause standards of IRC Section 6664(c).
Case Study 2: Independent Video Game and Simulation Studio Navigating Publisher-Funded Royalty Arrangements
Baseline Scenario and Legal Vulnerability

Aether Interactive, LLC ("Aether"), an independent software development studio founded by two graphics programmers, is developing a next-generation real-time fluid-dynamics and ray-tracing simulation engine integrated into an interactive video game title ("Project Titan"). Before commencing principal development, Aether enters into a "Development and Publishing Agreement" with Goliath Publishing Corp. ("Goliath"), an unrelated global video game distributor.

Under the initial agreement, Goliath agrees to advance $2.5 million to Aether in quarterly payments to cover Aether's development salaries and workstation hardware. Upon completion of the software, Goliath receives the exclusive worldwide right to manufacture, market, distribute, and sell Project Titan across all digital and retail platforms, paying Aether a 20% net royalty after Goliath recoups its $2.5 million advance. Aether has no internal marketing department, no publisher accounts on digital distribution platforms (such as Steam, PlayStation Network, or Epic Games Store), and never intends to market or sell the software itself. Relying on Rev. Proc. 2000-50, Aether claims the full $2.5 million under IRC Section 174 and claims $375,000 in federal R&D tax credits under IRC Section 41.

This structure triggers two fatal disqualifications under United States federal tax law. First, it violates the Saykally trade or business rule: as explicitly noted in industry tax analysis of Saykally v. Commissioner, 247 Fed. Appx. 914 (9th Cir. 2007), a software developer who develops software for a third party who then markets the software is not engaging in a trade or business involving the software and is ineligible for the Section 174 deduction. Because Aether ceded all marketing and sales functions to Goliath and intends solely to collect passive royalties, Aether fails both the "in connection with a trade or business" requirement of Section 174 and the stricter "carrying on a trade or business" requirement of Section 41(b)(1). Second, the arrangement violates the IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) funded research exclusion: because Goliath advances $2.5 million on a non-recourse basis (recoupable only out of future royalties) and Aether transfers exclusive exploitation rights to Goliath, the IRS will disallow the Section 41 credit on the ground that the research is "funded" by Goliath, as Aether neither bears the financial risk of failure nor retains "substantial rights" in the research under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d).
Step 1: Project Governance and Operational Capability Restructuring

To avoid the outcome in Saykally, where a developer who intended the technology to be marketed by another entity was found to lack the objective intent to use it in a trade or business of his own, Aether must establish verifiable self-publishing, direct-marketing, and multi-product engine licensing operations. Aether must restructure its corporate governance around two active commercial revenue pillars: first, the direct commercial licensing of its proprietary "Aether Fluid & Ray-Tracing Engine" middleware to other software studios, architectural visualization firms, and defense simulation contractors; and second, the co-publishing and direct digital sales of interactive software titles. Operationally, Aether must register and maintain active developer and publisher storefront accounts on major digital distribution platforms (e.g., Steamworks, Epic Games Store, and Apple App Store) in its own corporate name, retain a dedicated digital marketing coordinator, and sell downloadable content, PC versions, and commercial engine licenses directly to consumers and enterprise licensees. As reasoned in IRS LAFA 20055203F (which may not be used or cited as precedent), generating revenue streams from multiple independent sources with continuity and regularity proves that the taxpayer conducts an active trade or business for Section 174 purposes rather than functioning as a passive vehicle.
Step 2: Contractual Redesign to Satisfy Trade or Business Nexus and Unfunded Research Standards

Aether must renegotiate the Goliath agreement prior to execution to ensure Aether retains active commercialization roles, substantial IP rights, and full financial risk. First, to satisfy Saykally and the "substantial rights" mandate of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), the contract must explicitly stipulate that Aether retains 100% ownership, legal title, and commercial licensing rights to the underlying Aether Simulation Engine source code, tools, and algorithms, granting Goliath zero exclusivity over the underlying technology engine. Furthermore, rather than granting Goliath worldwide all-platform marketing exclusivity for Project Titan, Aether must retain direct self-publishing and marketing rights for PC digital distribution in North America, while appointing Goliath strictly as a console co-publisher or regional distribution service provider. Because Aether actively markets and sells the software itself in a primary commercial market, it can demonstrate the objective intent to use the fruits of its research in its own trade or business that the taxpayer in Saykally lacked.

Second, to defeat the Funded Research Exclusion under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), Aether must restructure the payment mechanics so that any development funding from Goliath is strictly contingent upon technical success and Aether bears the economic risk of technical failure. The contract must eliminate non-recourse royalty advances and instead tie milestone payments to objective, rigorous technical acceptance testing criteria—such as achieving 60 frames per second at 4K resolution with real-time Navier-Stokes particle collisions on target hardware. The agreement must explicitly mandate that if Aether fails to resolve the technical uncertainties and fails to deliver a software build meeting the contractual technical specifications, Goliath is not obligated to pay the milestone and Aether must refund any unapplied advances, thereby placing 100% of the financial risk of R&D failure squarely on Aether.
Step 3: Technical Documentation and Experimentation Tracking

To substantiate that Aether's software development expenses qualify under IRC Section 174 and Section 41, Aether must implement a contemporaneous technical documentation protocol aligned with the Four-Part Test. Crucially, under IRC Section 41(d)(3)(B) and Section 41(d)(4), research relating to style, taste, cosmetic design, or routine content creation is statutorily excluded. Aether must establish strict technical boundaries separating non-qualified artistic asset creation (storyboarding, voice acting, musical composition, and 3D character skinning) from qualified computer science experimentation (developing custom HLSL/GLSL ray-tracing shaders, spatial partitioning octrees, deterministic network netcode, and real-time GPU fluid solvers). For each qualified technical module, the lead graphics engineer must maintain bi-weekly Technical Uncertainty and Experimentation Reports integrated with Perforce or Git version control. These logs must document why standard off-the-shelf physics engines cannot simulate 500,000 interacting fluid particles within a 16.6-millisecond frame budget, and archive the iterative testing of code commits, GPU profiler frame-time captures, memory bandwidth bottlenecks, and mathematical adjustments to Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) kernels until target performance is achieved.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Time-Tracking, Wage Allocation, and Tax Compliance

To prevent the evidentiary disallowances and Section 6662 accuracy-related penalties seen in Saykally, Aether must implement a contemporaneous time-tracking system requiring all software engineers to log hours weekly by specific project code and technical activity, separating qualified engine experimentation from routine post-production debugging or artistic asset integration. Retrospective estimates or undocumented wage allocations are routinely rejected by the Tax Court. Finally, Aether's tax advisors must reconcile all Form W-2 Box 1 wages, qualified supply and cloud computing costs (ensuring hardware purchases are properly capitalized rather than misclassified as R&D supplies, a failure penalized in Betz v. Commissioner), and Section 174 schedules. This pre-filing review must verify zero double deductions between Section 174 and Section 162 and properly execute the IRC Section 280C(c) reduced credit election or deduction reduction on a timely filed return.
Strategic Conclusions for U.S. R&D Tax Practitioners

The Ninth Circuit's affirmance in Saykally v. Commissioner reinforces a foundational principle of United States R&D tax law: technical innovation and substantial financial expenditure are legally insufficient to sustain deductions under IRC Section 174 or tax credits under IRC Section 41 if the taxpayer claiming the tax benefit is structurally divorced from the active trade or business that commercializes the resulting technology. Whenever intellectual property development is separated from marketing and distribution—whether through founder-held sole proprietorships, special-purpose R&D entities, or third-party publishing agreements—tax advisors must verify prior to the commencement of research that the claiming entity possesses both the objective intent and the independent operational capability to exploit the research in its own active trade or business. By aligning entity governance, eliminating upfront exclusive licensing traps, maintaining strict intercompany accounting boundaries, and deploying contemporaneous technical and financial substantiation, taxpayers can insulate their R&D claims from examination challenges and secure the full statutory incentives enacted by Congress.
